events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025, art. 16
events.what_changed: Before: a residence was cancelled only after a conviction in Argentina for an intentional crime punishable by more than 5 years, or for repeat offending. There was a 2-year wait after the sentence, and a mandatory waiver for a parent, child or spouse of an Argentine. After: any conviction, in Argentina or abroad, for an intentional crime punishable by imprisonment, however served, leads to cancellation and expulsion. The waiver is discretionary, read restrictively, and barred for crimes against life, sexual integrity or the constitutional order. The protection is narrower, but the trigger is still a criminal conviction.

(Artículo sustituido por art. 16 del Decreto Nº 366/2025 B.O. 29/5/2025. Vigencia: a partir del día de su publicación en el BOLETÍN OFICIAL.)

events.instrument: Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia N° 366/2025, art. 8
events.what_changed: Before: entry and stay were barred for convictions or criminal records for named trafficking and money-laundering crimes, or crimes punishable by 3 years or more. A humanitarian or family-reunification exception was open. After: the bar also covers convictions for crimes punishable by less than 3 years, and being caught in flagrante for an offence eligible for probation. 'Condena' now includes a sentence that is not yet final, and 'antecedente' includes an indictment. The humanitarian exception is restrictive and excluded for crimes against life, sexual integrity or the constitutional order.

events.what_changed: Cancellation of a residence on the criminal grounds of art. 62 now always carries expulsion. Expulsion based on an intentional crime carries a permanent re-entry ban; before, the ban was graduated. This aggravates the consequences of a conviction.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: DNM figures obtained by Chequeado show about 1.2 expulsions a day of convicted foreigners ('extrañamiento de condenados'). That was a stable, moderate level under the 2004 thresholds, with the mandatory family waiver in force. I found no evidence of the rate of residence cancellations. 2025: expulsions rose to 620 in 2024 and to a record pace in early 2025. After DNU 366/2025 the government publicly promoted fast expulsions, before a final conviction, as 'extranjero que delinque se va'. The waiver is now restrictive. I rate the protection of residence status lower in 2026. The evidence counts expelled convicts; it does not directly measure cancellations of residence.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting citation attributes the trafficking and money-laundering list to art. 62(b). In the 2023 text that list is in art. 29(c), the bar on entry and stay. Art. 62(b) required a conviction for an intentional crime punishable by more than 5 years, or repeat offending. The family waiver for a parent, child or spouse of an Argentine was mandatory, not optional. The answer option itself holds.
answers.notes: For 2026 I keep the 50 option, but only just: since DNU 366/2025, any intentional crime punishable by imprisonment ends a residence, including minor ones and suspended sentences. Non-final convictions and indictments count for art. 29. Administrative or contravention offences still do not. I found no record that Congress rejected DNU 366/2025 under Ley 26.122, and InfoLEG shows it in force. The court rulings against it I saw (Juzgado Federal Paraná, Aug 2025; Cámara Nacional Electoral, 2026) concern Title III on citizenship, bind only the parties, and do not reach arts. 29 and 62. Decreto 681/2026 (B.O. 30/7/2026) later added hate-speech grounds to arts. 29 and 62. That is outside the window but matters for the November 2026 dossier.

answers.implementation_then_now: 2023: the US State Department's 2023 report says the government cooperated with UNHCR and had a working protection system. A search snippet attributes to UNHCR's 2023 report the finding of no confirmed refoulement, but I could not open that report. 2024-2025: the State Department's 2024 report repeats the same. CELS/CAREF (IACHR hearing, March 2025; shadow report to the UN Committee against Torture, Nov 2025) and Committee members at the November 2025 review raised concerns that DNU 942/2024 and the move of migration to the Ministry of Security put non-refoulement at risk. Members cited fewer appeal routes and the loss of suspensive effect. No documented case of refoulement to torture was found for either period, so I keep the rating unchanged at the starting 'Sometimes'.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The strongest statutory basis is Ley 26.165 art. 7. It expressly bars the expulsion, return or extradition of refugees and asylum seekers where there is a risk of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The starting citation lists it but quotes only Ley 25.871 art. 29 and Decreto 616/2010. With no documented refoulement in 2023, 'Usually' may fit the 2023 practice better than 'Sometimes'.
answers.notes: The answer stays 'Yes' on both dates: art. 7 of Ley 26.165, Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m) and the constitutional treaties are unchanged. I chose 'not the same' rather than 'no change' because one cited provision (Ley 25.871 art. 29) was replaced, and DNU 942/2024 narrowed who counts as a refugee under art. 7. DNU 942/2024 also cut the appeal deadline to 5 working days (art. 50). I found no congressional rejection of either DNU.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting citation cites Ley 26.165 'Article 29', which concerns CONARE's functions. The relevant provision is art. 7, which protects life, liberty and security of the person. Ley 25.871 art. 29 itself does not mention humanitarian assistance in expulsion. Its humanitarian clause is an exception allowing admission despite the bars.
answers.notes: The answer is 'Yes' on both dates. The change classification is driven by the replacement of the cited art. 29 by DNU 366/2025 and by DNU 942/2024's narrower exclusion clause. Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m), the core basis for non-refugees, did not change.
